candidato.titulo: What are biomarkers? How doctors assess health and pooling people's cells reveals new markers—a biologist explains
candidato.resumo: A family of five is exposed to the flu virus, but only two of them get sick. A lifelong chain-smoker lives 100 years, while a professional athlete in their prime dies of an unexpected heart attack. A drug fails a clinical trial due to harmful side effects in a subset of patients despite showing good results in others.

texto_fonte:
What are biomarkers? How doctors assess health and pooling people's cells reveals new markers—a biologist explains
A family of five is exposed to the flu virus, but only two of them get sick. A lifelong chain-smoker lives 100 years, while a professional athlete in their prime dies of an unexpected heart attack. A drug fails a clinical trial due to harmful side effects in a subset of patients despite showing good results in others.
Could any of these scenarios have been predicted? The simple answer is not yet—but perhaps soon with the help of biomarkers.
A biomarker is anything measurable in the body that gives clinicians insight into someone's current or future health. Biomarkers come in many forms and play a critical role in modern medicine by shedding light on the inner workings of the human body.
Many biomarkers are measured during routine procedures at the doctor's office, including through blood tests and vital signs.
Physiological biomarkers such as heart rate and blood oxygen levels indicate how well your body is functioning. Cellular biomarkers such as white blood cell count provide useful information on the activity of your immune system. Genetic biomarkers are parts of your DNA that provide clues about your inherent risk of developing a particular disease or how likely you are to respond to a treatment.
There are still many more biomarkers to be discovered, and researchers are devising unique ways to identify a person's risk of disease.
Discovering new biomarkers
The traditional way researchers identify biomarkers is by asking which biological features differ between two or more groups. This might look like comparing patients with a specific disease with healthy volunteers, people who respond to a drug with people who don't, or the same group of people at two different points in time.
Many biomarker discoveries started with observations made in laboratories. For example, doctors use hemoglobin A1c levels in the blood to test for diabetes. The origins of this test date back to the 1960s, when scientists found abnormally high levels of a protein in the blood of people with diabetes. Repeated testing in the clinic over the next few decades confirmed the relationship between A1c levels and diabetes, culminating in the Food and Drug Administration approving the first A1c-based diabetes diagnostic test in 2013.
Other biomarkers that also started with observations made through basic research in the lab include screening tests for colorectal cancer, drug metabolism and inherited metabolic diseases in newborns.
Genetic biomarkers are typically found by scanning the genomes of thousands to even millions of people for genetic variants linked to a trait or disease. This approach is called a genomewide association study. This method has resulted in many important biomarkers that provide guidance on how to manage a patient's risk of heart disease, age-related vision loss and liver disease.
One limitation of using the genomewide association study, though, is that it does not always provide information on which tissue or cell types may be relevant to the genetic variant. This lack of cellular information could be solved with cell cultures that allow researchers to study specific cell types under controlled conditions outside the body.
Human populations in a dish
In my work as a neuroscientist and geneticist, I take a different approach to finding biomarkers in the lab: I conduct genomewide association studies on human brain cells in a dish to understand how cells change when they encounter harmful exposures such as toxins and viruses.
Cells are the building blocks of all human tissues and organ systems. How sensitive they are to different environmental factors can greatly affect a person's health and disease risk.
Thanks to revolutions in stem cell technologies, scientists are now able to model the effects of the environment on many different cell types—including brain cells that are nearly impossible to study in living people without causing irreversible damage to the brain. Instead, my colleagues and I obtain stem cells created from the blood or skin of human donors and convert them to brain cells for our experiments.
Most studies focus on how cells from only a handful of people respond to environmental stressors, mainly because it is quite difficult to conduct experiments at the population scale in a petri dish. To know whose cells are in a dish, researchers traditionally needed to handle and maintain cells from different people separately. This requirement adds considerable time, effort and cost for every new cell line included in the experimental design.
Because these issues limit the scale of experiments, studies aren't able to capture the natural diversity of people and therefore cannot answer questions about why an exposure might make one person sick but have no effect on another.
My laboratory tackles this problem by pooling stem cell–derived brain cells from dozens to hundreds of people into the same culture dish—what my team calls a cell village. We use the genomes of these cells as natural barcodes to determine who donated each one. We then add different environmental perturbations to the village—such as pathogens, chemical pollutants and radiation—and measure how each person's cells react.
Each cell might respond by turning on or off a set of genes, showing an increased or decreased propensity to die, or doing nothing at all. Identifying which genes are linked to these particular responses can help explain why a person's cells respond the way they do.
These genes are essentially biomarkers for the vulnerability of a specific cell type to an exposure.
An atlas of human vulnerability
While cell villages are relatively new, they have already helped researchers better understand what makes people different from each other.
For example, my team and I used cell villages to identify a biomarker that indicates a person may be particularly vulnerable to Zika virus infection. Zika is a pathogen spread by mosquitoes that can cause neurological disorders and microcephaly—small head size—in developing fetuses. Using stem cell–derived brain cells from 40 people, we found that not everyone was equally susceptible to infection. For some, fewer than 1% of their cells were infected by Zika virus; for others, it was greater than 99%.
Through additional cell village experiments, we discovered a genetic variant that regulates a powerful antiviral gene called IFITM3. In this case, the cells of a person with version A of this gene were more vulnerable to infection than the cells of a person with version B. Researchers have found links between this same genetic variant and COVID-19 and influenza A infection severity, suggesting it could be a genetic biomarker that can predict how certain people may respond to certain types of pathogens.
My team has also conducted similar work to identify genetic biomarkers for a person's sensitivity to lead, a pervasive neurodevelopmental toxin. We are also using cell villages to find biomarkers for a person's vulnerability to PFAS, also known as forever chemicals; measles virus infection; and stress hormones.
Our goal is to build what we call an atlas of human vulnerability: a catalog of genetic biomarkers to predict how each person might respond at the cellular level to a wide range of harmful exposures.
The future of biomarkers
The cell village is only one of many emerging technologies that could usher in a new era of biomarker detection.
As DNA sequencing costs continue to drop, whole genome sequencing could become more routine in the clinic and potentially improve the ability to find links between genes and health outcomes that health care teams can intervene in.
Researchers are developing AI tools to survey medical imaging such as CT and MRI scans with the intention of finding new biomarkers for cancer progression that would have likely gone unnoticed by the human eye.
Cellphones and smartwatches may also be useful in efforts to discover new health-related biomarkers. For example, some studies have used these and other wearable devices to find behavioral biomarkers that predict major depressive episodes.
The goal now is to test how well these biomarkers work in the real world and make them widely available so that doctors everywhere can have as much information as possible about their patients when making life-changing decisions.
Publication details
Michael F. Wells et al., Natural variation in gene expression and viral susceptibility revealed by neural progenitor cell villages, Cell Stem Cell (2023). DOI: 10.1016/j.stem.2023.01.010
Journal information: Cell Stem Cell

candidato.titulo: Molecular structures reveal how a bacteriophage protein inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis
candidato.resumo: Drug-resistant bacteria are becoming more common worldwide, posing a major public health challenge. Addressing this problem requires finding new ways to eliminate bacteria, which in turn requires analyzing essential cellular processes that could serve as targets for future antibiotics.

texto_fonte:
Molecular structures reveal how a bacteriophage protein inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis
Drug-resistant bacteria are becoming more common worldwide, posing a major public health challenge. Addressing this problem requires finding new ways to eliminate bacteria, which in turn requires analyzing essential cellular processes that could serve as targets for future antibiotics.
Nature may offer some clues in viruses known as bacteriophages, or "phages." These viruses infect bacteria and hijack their cellular machinery to replicate. Some of them even inject small proteins that shut down specific bacterial processes, ultimately causing the cell to die.
One target is MurJ, a protein that bacteria use to transport lipids needed to build their cell wall. Although several bacteriophage proteins that can inhibit MurJ have been found, their amino acid sequences can be quite varied. How can such different proteins block the same essential target, and do they use the same molecular strategy?
Examining a phage protein's grip on MurJ
To answer these questions, a research team led by Assistant Professor Hidetaka Kohga of Nara Institute of Science and Technology (NAIST), Japan, examined how a bacteriophage protein called SglPP7 inhibits MurJ.
Their study, which was published in PLOS Biology, reveals the finer details of how SglPP7 interacts with MurJ and compares its inhibition mechanism with those of other phage proteins that target the same lipid transporter.
Co-authors include Kaito Hosoda, Sixian Wu, Hiroyuki Tanaka, Dr. Hideki Shigematsu, Assistant Professor Ryoji Miyazaki, Associate Professor Min Fey Chek and Professor Tomoya Tsukazaki, all from NAIST.
The researchers used cryo-electron microscopy, a technique that reveals the structures of biological molecules at near-atomic resolution, to determine the structure of the MurJ–SglPP7 complex. They also performed experiments involving targeted protein mutations, bacterial cell lysis and computer simulations to investigate how the interaction with SglPP7 affects MurJ's behavior.
Different proteins lock MurJ in place
The results showed that SglPP7 lies along a lipid-binding groove in MurJ and inserts its short C-terminal tail into a deep internal cavity. This interaction stabilizes MurJ in an outward-facing conformation, preventing it from completing the back-and-forth structural changes required to transport lipid.
Comparisons with two other known phage proteins, LysM and SglCJ3, revealed that all three stabilize a similar conformation of MurJ despite binding to it in different ways. "These findings suggest convergent evolution toward a common target through diverse inhibitory mechanisms," says Kohga.
Understanding these interactions could help researchers design new drugs and engineer artificial phage proteins with targeted antibacterial activity. "By revealing how phage proteins inhibit MurJ, this study provides a foundation for drug discovery targeting this transporter," explains Kohga.
"Although still at the basic research stage, these findings could contribute to the development of new antibacterial agents against drug-resistant bacteria."
Further research efforts in this field will hopefully shed light on antibacterial mechanisms that evolved naturally and bring us closer to a new generation of antibiotics.
Publication details
Kaito Hosoda et al., Structural basis for inhibition of the lipid flippase MurJ by phage lysis protein SglPP7 suggests convergent evolution with other Sgl peptides, PLOS Biology (2026). DOI: 10.1371/journal.pbio.3004039

candidato.titulo: Why predictive maintenance matters more as factories add robots
candidato.resumo: As robotics scales across industries, companies need a maintenance strategy to collect and use the right data to minimize downtime. The post Why predictive maintenance matters more as factories add robots appeared first on The Robot Report .

texto_fonte:
Factories are adding more robots because they can handle repetitive, precise, and physically demanding work at high speed. As robotics take on a greater share of production, keeping those systems available becomes more important.
The International Federation of Robotics (IFR) reported about 5 million industrial robots in operation worldwide in 2025, up 11% from the prior year.
An unexpected robot failure can affect more than one machine. It can interrupt a cell, slow a line, and create delays that spread through the plant. As manufacturers rely more heavily on robotic systems, the need to identify developing problems before they force equipment offline becomes increasingly valuable.
Why robotic systems raise the support stakes
Traditional preventive maintenance follows a schedule based on time, usage, or manufacturer recommendations. That approach still has value, but it may not reveal what’s happening inside a robot between planned service intervals. A joint, reducer, motor, or controller can begin to show signs of wear while the robot is still operating.
Predictive maintenance uses equipment data to identify changes that may point to developing faults. NIST describes condition monitoring as the detection, diagnosis or prediction of faults and failures in industrial equipment.
For robotics, that means maintenance decisions can be based more on actual equipment condition than on a calendar alone.
What predictive maintenance can monitor
Industrial automation and related systems generate many types of operating data. Useful signals depend on the robot, application, and failure mode. Common examples include vibration, temperature, and motor current. Torque, controller alarms, cycle data, and maintenance history can also provide useful context.
The goal isn’t to collect every available data point. Teams need data that can reveal changes tied to the way a robot operates. A rise in vibration may point to a mechanical issue, while changes in motor current or torque may indicate added resistance or abnormal loading. Temperature variations can also signal that a component isn’t operating as expected.
Changes in an end effector, sensor, conveyor, or surrounding process can affect robot performance. Looking at the robot in the context of a larger workcell can help teams separate normal operating variation from a change that may deserve maintenance attention. That distinction is especially important if the same robot handles different loads, speeds, or motion paths.
This is where reliability monitoring can help. Sensors and connected systems can gather machine data, while monitoring and analytics tools help identify changes in equipment behavior. When a pattern changes, maintenance teams can then investigate the cause before a failure forces the robot offline.
Turn robot data into maintenance decisions
Collecting data is only the first step. The information has to support a practical maintenance decision. A useful alert should help a team determine what needs attention, how urgent the issue is, and when the robot can be inspected without causing an unnecessary production interruption.
This becomes more important as factories operate larger fleets of robots. Maintenance teams may not have time to inspect every asset at the same frequency. Predictive maintenance can help direct attention toward equipment showing signs of change while allowing healthy assets to remain in service.
Earlier warnings can also improve parts planning. If a component shows signs of deterioration, teams may have more time to confirm the problem, locate the correct replacement part, and schedule work during a planned maintenance window.
Getting ahead on productivity, asset life, and safety
The value of predictive maintenance goes beyond preventing unplanned stops. Finding issues early on can limit secondary damage and help manufacturers get more useful life from robotic assets. Planned repairs can also reduce the disruption that occurs when technicians must troubleshoot a failed robot during production.
A planned maintenance window gives teams more control over when equipment is taken offline and serviced. That can support safer maintenance practices because technicians can prepare for the work instead of responding to an unexpected failure under production pressure.
As more factories rely heavily on robotics, maintenance strategies need to account for how those systems perform throughout their service life. Predictive maintenance gives manufacturers a way to use equipment data, condition signals and analytics to identify developing issues earlier. When that information leads to timely inspection and repair, manufacturers can reduce unplanned downtime, protect robotic assets and keep production schedules more stable.
About the author
Rob Carbone is vice president of operations at Advanced Technology Services. He is responsible for leading initiatives that help manufacturers improve equipment reliability, maintenance excellence, and customer success.

texto_fonte:
Anthropic lança Claude Fable 5.2, supera Opus 5.5 e libera uso extra para assinantes
Por Viviane França |
A Anthropic anunciou o Claude Fable 5.2, novo modelo de inteligência artificial que supera o Opus 5.5 e concorrentes em testes de programação, engenharia de software, pesquisa científica e raciocínio. A ferramenta já está disponível para assinantes de planos pagos e também pode ser acessada pelas plataformas Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud e Microsoft Azure.
O modelo alcançou 49,1% no benchmark FrontierCode 2.0, que avalia programação com agentes de IA, contra 45,5% do Opus 5.5 e 42,8% do GPT-6 Astra. Na engenharia de software, obteve 69,9% no FrontierSWE v2, acima do Fable 5.1 (56,3%) e do Opus 5.5 (62,3%). Já no teste OSWorld 2.1, que avalia o controle de computadores, atingiu 89,3%.
Os resultados também incluem avanços em pesquisa científica e raciocínio. No Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, o Fable 5.2 obteve 74,6%, enquanto o Opus 5.5 registrou 58,7%. O novo modelo ainda alcançou 74,2% no Humanity's Last Exam e 73,4% no Chartography, que avalia o reconhecimento de informações visuais. Segundo a Anthropic, ele também executa tarefas complexas com menos tokens e gera respostas até 30% mais rápido que o Fable 5.1.
O Fable 5.2 também demonstrou capacidade de executar projetos práticos, que vão além de responder a perguntas. Em testes, o modelo projetou e programou dispositivos eletrônicos funcionais, como um assistente de voz e um bichinho virtual, controlou braços robóticos para abrir garrafas e resolver quebra-cabeças e ajudou cientistas em cálculos complexos sobre buracos negros. Segundo a Anthropic, o modelo é indicado para projetos técnicos ambiciosos, e o Claude Opus 5.5 continua recomendado para tarefas cotidianas.
A empresa também apresentou o Claude Mythos 5.2, versão baseada no Fable 5.2, mas com menos restrições de uso. O modelo foi desenvolvido para tarefas avançadas de segurança cibernética e pesquisas biomédicas. O acesso, porém, é restrito a organizações aprovadas pelos programas de verificação da Anthropic para essas duas áreas.
Anthropic libera uso extra do Claude Fable 5.2 para assinantes
Para marcar o lançamento, a Anthropic liberou limites adicionais de uso do Fable 5.2 para assinantes elegíveis. Durante esta semana, os usuários receberão de uma a três redefinições extras dos limites, de acordo com o tempo de assinatura.
Além disso, o modelo foi incluído em até 50% dos limites semanais dos planos Pro e dos assentos padrão do Team. A medida vale para o claude.ai e o Claude Code e facilita os testes da ferramenta em tarefas exigentes.
O acesso pela API, para desenvolvedores e empresas, custa US$ 8 por milhão de tokens de entrada e US$ 40 por milhão de tokens de saída. Há também um modo rápido, que acelera a geração em até 2,5 vezes e cobra US$ 16 e US$ 80 por milhão de tokens, respectivamente. Para usuários individuais, o acesso ocorre pelos planos de assinatura da Anthropic, sem cobrança por milhão de tokens.

texto_fonte:
AMD lança CPU gigante de 256 núcleos para deixar NVIDIA e Intel preocupadas
Por Léo Müller |
A AMD apresentou todos os detalhes da sexta geração dos seus processadores EPYC na última quarta-feira (4), durante um evento fechado para a imprensa. Os novos EPYC Venice são chips literalmente gigantes — como você pode ver na imagem abaixo — e reúnem até 256 núcleos e 512 threads para atender à crescente demanda por inteligência artificial agêntica nos data centers de grandes empresas de tecnologia.
Segundo os testes de benchmark apresentados ao Canaltech durante o AMD In Depth 2026, em Las Vegas, nos Estados Unidos, os novos processadores demonstraram vantagens consideráveis sobre alternativas da NVIDIA e da Intel em determinadas aplicações de IA.
Em um dos cenários, a fabricante afirma que o Venice consegue executar até 2,8 vezes mais agentes de inteligência artificial por watt consumido do que soluções concorrentes. Isso é motivo suficiente para deixar a concorrência preocupada com market-share em um mercado que drena bilhões de dólares da economia global mensalmente.
A AMD também divulgou resultados de uma plataforma que combina os novos EPYC Venice com aceleradores gráficos Instinct. Nesse caso, a empresa afirma entregar até 30% mais tokens de IA por dólar investido em comparação com a plataforma NVIDIA Vera Rubin, indicando que a disputa entre as fabricantes vai muito além da potência bruta dos processadores.
EPYC Venice estreia arquitetura Zen 6 com até 256 núcleos
Os novos processadores representam a sexta geração da família EPYC e utilizam a arquitetura Zen 6, que estreia uma nova etapa na evolução dos chips para servidores da AMD. A linha traz configurações com até 256 núcleos Zen 6c e 512 threads, oferecendo uma capacidade de processamento paralelo voltada especialmente à execução simultânea de milhares de tarefas.
Os modelos também utilizam chiplets fabricados com tecnologia de 2 nanômetros da TSMC, além de uma arquitetura de interconexão e memória desenvolvida para acompanhar o aumento na quantidade de núcleos.
A chegada dos EPYC Venice já era aguardada desde julho, quando a AMD confirmou que a arquitetura Zen 6 estrearia nos processadores para servidores antes dos novos Ryzen para computadores pessoais.
Agora, a fabricante revelou uma família completa de produtos, incluindo versões otimizadas para desempenho máximo, eficiência energética, aplicações corporativas e computação científica.
Entre os principais avanços estão o suporte a até 16 canais de memória DDR5, largura de banda teórica de até 1,6 TB/s, conexões PCI Express 6.0 e compatibilidade com a tecnologia CXL 3.1, utilizada para expandir a capacidade de memória dos servidores.
Há ainda o Venice-X, versão equipada com tecnologia 3D V-Cache e até 1.152 MB de cache L3, e modelos de alta frequência que chegam a 5,3 GHz, voltados principalmente a sistemas que precisam alimentar aceleradores de inteligência artificial com grandes volumes de dados.
AMD promete superar Intel e NVIDIA na execução de agentes de IA
A principal aposta da AMD para justificar tantos núcleos está na mudança que a inteligência artificial vem provocando dentro dos data centers.
Até recentemente, boa parte da atenção da indústria estava concentrada nas GPUs, responsáveis pelo treinamento e pela execução de modelos generativos. Entretanto, o crescimento da IA agêntica está aumentando a importância dos processadores convencionais.
Diferentemente de um chatbot que apenas responde perguntas, um agente de IA pode acessar bancos de dados, executar programas, consultar ferramentas, realizar operações e interagir com outros agentes para concluir tarefas.
Grande parte dessas atividades depende diretamente das CPUs. Por isso, a AMD acredita que os novos servidores precisarão combinar GPUs cada vez mais poderosas com processadores capazes de lidar com um número crescente de operações simultâneas.
Durante o evento, Dan McNamara, vice-presidente sênior e gerente-geral da divisão de Computação e IA Empresarial da AMD, destacou que a nova geração foi desenvolvida especificamente para essa transformação.
"Passamos de milhões de usuários humanos para bilhões de usos por agentes. E cada um deles passa por ciclos de execução que aumentam exponencialmente a demanda por computação", explicou o executivo.
Nos testes apresentados pela fabricante, os EPYC Venice alcançaram uma pontuação relativa de 1,7 em agentes de IA executados por watt, contra 0,6 da NVIDIA Vera e 0,8 dos Xeon de sexta geração da Intel.
Isso representa uma vantagem de aproximadamente 2,8 vezes sobre a solução da NVIDIA e 2,1 vezes sobre a alternativa da Intel no cenário avaliado.
A AMD também afirma que seu novo sistema de gerenciamento de energia, chamado Unified Power Provisioning (UPP), pode ampliar ainda mais essa vantagem, elevando o ganho máximo de eficiência para 3,3 vezes em determinados cenários.
É importante destacar que os resultados foram divulgados pela própria fabricante e dependem das configurações utilizadas, além das características específicas das aplicações executadas.
AMD quer entregar mais desempenho gastando menos energia
O consumo energético está entre as maiores preocupações das empresas que operam data centers de inteligência artificial. Quanto mais servidores são instalados, maiores são os custos com eletricidade, refrigeração e infraestrutura.
Por isso, a AMD desenvolveu diferentes versões do Venice para atender a necessidades específicas, em vez de apostar somente em processadores com o maior número possível de núcleos.
Um exemplo é o EPYC Venice HF, que reúne 96 núcleos e pode alcançar frequências de até 5,3 GHz. Sua função é trabalhar como processador principal de servidores equipados com aceleradores gráficos, garantindo que as GPUs recebam os dados necessários sem ficarem ociosas.
"Você quer que seus aceleradores sejam bem aproveitados. Não quer que eles fiquem parados enquanto esperam que a CPU os atenda", explicou McNamara durante a apresentação.
A fabricante também desenvolveu o Verano, uma variante da nova família com foco em eficiência energética e suporte a até 192 núcleos e 384 threads, além de memória LPDDR5X.
Como o Canaltech já havia antecipado em uma reportagem sobre os novos processadores AMD EPYC Verano com memória LPDDR5X e até 192 núcleos, a proposta é aproveitar memórias de baixo consumo para reduzir os gastos energéticos em instalações de grande escala.
Os novos processadores ainda serão utilizados no ecossistema Helion, uma arquitetura de referência para racks de servidores de inteligência artificial que permite reunir dezenas de milhares de núcleos Zen 6 em uma única instalação.
Benchmarks mostram vantagem sobre Xeon e Vera Rubin
Além dos resultados em inteligência artificial agêntica, a AMD apresentou comparações de desempenho em aplicações empresariais tradicionais.
Em um conjunto de oito cargas de trabalho voltadas a serviços de nuvem, os EPYC Venice teriam alcançado desempenho de até 3,3 vezes o apresentado pelos Xeon de sexta geração da Intel, segundo os dados divulgados pela fabricante.
O mesmo multiplicador apareceu em um conjunto de seis aplicações relacionadas a armazenamento e bancos de dados. Já em cinco aplicações empresariais, a vantagem anunciada chegou a 2,6 vezes.
Na execução de modelos de IA, a AMD apresentou outra comparação envolvendo os novos processadores. Uma plataforma equipada com EPYC Venice e GPUs Instinct teria conseguido entregar até 30% mais tokens por dólar do que a solução NVIDIA Vera Rubin, segundo os testes internos da empresa.
A empresa também destacou que a sexta geração dos EPYC oferece até 12 vezes mais capacidade de consolidação de servidores em um dos cenários de modernização apresentados, reduzindo a quantidade de máquinas necessárias para executar determinadas cargas de trabalho.
Apesar dos números expressivos, os resultados não representam uma vitória absoluta sobre Intel ou NVIDIA. O desempenho real dependerá do tipo de aplicação, da configuração dos servidores e das condições de operação.
Nova geração também promete reduzir custos com memória RAM
Outra novidade apresentada durante o evento foi a MEXT Memory, uma tecnologia desenvolvida pela AMD para reduzir a necessidade de memória RAM convencional em servidores.
A solução combina DRAM com armazenamento flash em SSDs NVMe, utilizando inteligência artificial para prever quais dados precisarão ser acessados pelo processador.
Em testes realizados com a nova geração EPYC Venice, a tecnologia conseguiu preservar 99% do desempenho em uma média de aplicações com agentes de IA, mesmo utilizando apenas metade da quantidade original de DRAM.
A AMD acredita que a combinação entre processadores com mais núcleos e tecnologias capazes de reduzir o custo de memória pode tornar a construção e a operação de data centers consideravelmente mais econômicas.
Embora os novos processadores tenham sido desenvolvidos para servidores corporativos, seus avanços também ilustram como a corrida pela inteligência artificial está transformando o mercado de semicondutores.
Com até 256 núcleos em um único chip e resultados expressivos de desempenho por watt, a AMD quer mostrar que a próxima etapa da inteligência artificial dependerá tanto das CPUs quanto das GPUs — e que a companhia pretende disputar esse mercado diretamente com Intel e NVIDIA.
* O Canaltech viajou à Las Vegas a convite da AMD.

candidato.titulo: See the first images from the new ZWO Seestar S30 Plus — a smart telescope aimed at beginners
candidato.resumo: While rivals announce increasingly expensive smart telescopes, ZWO’s new Seestar S30 Plus makes galaxy and nebula photography surprisingly affordable.

texto_fonte:
As rival makers announce increasingly ambitious smart telescopes, ZWO has taken a different approach. Its new Seestar S30 Plus launched today and is available for $474 from Seestar’s website and Amazon, just in time for Christmas. Better still, we’ve been using it for a month and can bring you a first look.
Announced a few months after the flagship Seestar S50 Pro and replacing the now-discontinued Seestar S30, the new Seestar S30 Plus retains its 30mm aperture and compact chassis, but upgrades to four-element apochromatic optics with extra-low dispersion (ED) glass and two 3.7-megapixel cameras.
Both produce 1,440 x 2,560-pixel images, while a much-improved 43.5-degree wide-angle camera can capture the Milky Way, constellations, star trails and nightscapes. Built-in filters, a mosaic mode and equatorial (EQ) tracking add considerable deep-sky astrophotography potential.
For a telescope weighing just 3.64 lbs (1.65 kg), it’s impressive. It easily fits into a camera bag and could happily live on a bookshelf.
I’ve already photographed the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), the Pleiades (M45), the Dumbbell Nebula (M27) and the North America Nebula (NGC 7000). The results are excellent for such a small instrument, especially when imaging nebulas with its built-in dual-band filter, which helps reduce light pollution.
The Seestar app adds new in-app post-processing options, so you don’t have to mess around with any of that — though you can also export everything as lossless FITS files. The S30 Plus also includes a magnetic solar filter, enabling you to indulge in solar photography safely.
With Dwarflab’s $1,299 Draco (3.5-inch/90mm aperture) recently landed in stores and Vaonis’ own $4,990 Atlas (3.1-inch/80mm aperture) not available until 2027, ZWO’s decision to offer an upgraded entry-level smart telescope that buyers can get their hands on right now looks particularly smart.
With ZWO's pattern of delivering cheaper smart telescopes without sacrificing on quality, the Seestar S30 Plus could be one of Christmas 2026’s best gifts for anyone interested in astronomy — and maybe that’s the point of it. Either way, first impressions are good. A full review is coming tomorrow, so check back at Space.com to find out our full thoughts and testing.
Breaking space news, the latest updates on rocket launches, skywatching events and more!
Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

candidato.titulo: Professor Emeritus Jeffrey Goldstone, highly influential theoretical physicist, dies at 93
candidato.resumo: An MIT faculty member for nearly half a century, Goldstone was a “theoretical physicist of rare talent and impact” who made fundamental contributions to multiple disciplines.

texto_fonte:
Eminent theoretical physicist Jeffrey Goldstone, an MIT professor emeritus, Dirac Medalist, and holder of the Department of Physics’ Cecil and Ida Green chair, died Oct. 12 at age 93.
A member of the MIT physics community for 49 years, Goldstone was especially known for his influential work in quantum field theory as well as contributions to quantum optimization algorithms. Notably, he is the namesake of the Goldstone boson and the related Goldstone theorem.
“Jeffrey was a giant of theoretical physics who will be long remembered and very much missed,” says Tracy Slatyer, director of the MIT Center for Theoretical Physics – a Leinweber Institute (CTP-LI) and professor of physics. “He contributed greatly to the CTP-LI over the years, and it was an honor to have him as a colleague.”
“Goldstone was a brilliant theoretical physicist and a charming, yet diffident and remarkably humble human being,” says Frank Wilczek, a CTP-LI colleague who is the Herman Feshbach Professor of Physics, Emeritus, and a 2004 Nobel laureate. “He made renowned, fundamental contributions to diverse areas of physics, ranging from condensed matter and quantum computing to string theory. Throughout, you can perceive a consistent style: enormous mathematical talent brought to bear on important, concrete, sharply posed physical problems.”
Goldstone is renowned for his remarkable range of groundbreaking discoveries. He began his career as a nuclear theorist. In his early work on nuclear matter with Hans Bethe, he developed the use of Feynman diagrams for non-relativistic many-fermion systems.
He later turned to particle physics, investigating relativistic field theories with spontaneously broken symmetries. Building on ideas inspired by superconductivity, he demonstrated that spontaneously broken continuous symmetries must be accompanied by massless, spinless particles — now widely known as Goldstone bosons (or Nambu-Goldstone bosons, in recognition of Yoichiro Nambu’s earlier related insights).
In subsequent work with Abdus Salam and Steven Weinberg, Goldstone formalized and generalized this result, which became known as the Goldstone theorem. With Claudio Rebbi, Charles Thorn, and Peter Goddard, he worked out the light-cone quantization of relativistic strings, a foundational result in string theory. Goldstone also worked with Roman Jackiw and Frank Wilczek on solitons in quantum field theory.
Goldstone was born in 1933 in Manchester, England. He earned his PhD from Trinity College at the University of Cambridge in 1958 and completed postdoctoral work at Cambridge, Harvard University, CERN, and Copenhagen University. After shifting his focus to particle theory, he joined the faculty at Cambridge in 1962. He moved to MIT as a professor of physics in 1977 and as a researcher in the Laboratory for Nuclear Science, and was appointed the Cecil and Ida Green Professor of Physics in 1983. Goldstone served as director of the Center for Theoretical Physics (now known as the CTP-LI) from 1983 to 1989.
“Goldstone’s name will always be associated with spontaneous symmetry breaking, where 'Goldstone’s theorem' and 'Goldstone bosons' feature prominently,” Wilczek notes. “His early, seminal papers relating the mathematical concept to physical phenomena gave firm foundations upon which people built fruitful theories of magnetism, meson physics, and eventually the Standard Model and early universe cosmology.
“Jeffrey Goldstone’s ideas are so deeply woven into physics that it takes an occasion like his passing to remind us how much we owe him. I had the pleasure to work with Jeffrey in the early days of fractional charge. The short paper we wrote together is one that I’m especially proud of. It contains the seeds of many later developments. Thank you, Jeffrey, for that fond memory.”
Alan Guth ’69, PhD ’72, MIT’s Victor F. Weisskopf Professor of Physics, Post-Tenure, says, “Jeffrey was a wonderful friend and colleague, and a towering figure in theoretical physics. When I was trying to arrange to come back to MIT after being a postdoc for nine years at other places, it was Jeffrey who I contacted to try to make this happen. When I first learned in 1981 that Andrei Linde had figured out how to make cosmic inflation work, in the form known as 'new inflation,’ I remember that I ran into Jeffrey's office to share my excitement. I have learned a great deal from Jeffrey over the years, and will forever have warm memories of our friendship.”
“Jeffrey Goldstone was a theoretical physicist of rare talent and impact,” says David Kaiser, MIT professor of physics and the Germeshausen Professor of the History of Science. “His landmark article, 'Field theories with superconductor solutions,' published in 1961, helped to launch the modern era of symmetry breaking in high-energy physics. Building on insights from neighboring fields such as condensed-matter physics, Goldstone demonstrated that for any model in which a continuous symmetry is spontaneously broken, there will emerge zero-mass, zero-spin particles now known as 'Goldstone bosons.' His watershed study, and several influential follow-up articles, have become central to our Standard Model of particle physics, with further application as far afield as early-universe cosmology to spin waves in magnetic materials and quantized vibrations in excited fluids. Later in his career, Goldstone turned his attention to quantum information science, helping to construct several novel algorithms for quantum computation.
“Typically reserved, his close friends admired his droll humor. Writing to Harvard physicist Sidney Coleman in November 1976, for example, Goldstone declined Coleman’s invitation to attend an upcoming physics workshop. 'I expect to be in total confusion during January [1977] and wish to simplify my life,’ Goldstone replied. 'Forty-three years in the womb’ — including decades at his alma mater, the University of Cambridge — 'have unfitted me for coping with normal trivial details of survival. It’s probably a good thing I’m coming out, but the birth pangs are hell.’
“The birthing event to which Goldstone referred was his move to MIT to join the Physics Department faculty in 1977. Thank goodness he braved the move. Over nearly 50 years, Jeffrey Goldstone enriched our Department of Physics at MIT, and especially our Center for Theoretical Physics – A Leinweber Institute, with his deep insights and gentle manner.”
Even after retiring from MIT, he remained active in research for the next two decades, working in quantum computation.
Edward Farhi, professor emeritus of physics and a frequent collaborator for over 20 years, describes Goldstone’s contribution to the field from its early stages as “very significant.”
“FFG [Farhi, Goldstone, and Samuel Gutmann] teamed up with Donner Professor of Mathematics Michael Sipser and showed that there was a problem which could not be sped up with a quantum computer, learning parity in the oracle setting,” Farhi says. “This was the first demonstration of this kind of limitation, although the same week another group proved the same thing by a different method. In 2000 FGG, along with Sipser, introduced the concept of Quantum Computation by Adiabatic Evolution. This is an all-purpose approach to optimization and was later shown to be universal, which means that any quantum computation can be encoded as quantum adiabatic. Furthermore, the company D-wave was founded to run this algorithm. D-wave is the progenitor of all of the superconducting hardware efforts such at the ones at Google and IBM. We later showed that using scattering theory a quantum computer could determine who wins a game provably faster than the best classical algorithm for this task.
“FGG introduced the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm. This was the first time a general purpose quantum optimizer could provide worst-case performance guarantees for combinatorial optimization problems. These guarantees as of now (with one exception) do not beat the best classical. Still, this paper has over 6,000 citations, making QAOA one the most-studied quantum algorithms.
“In 2019, FGG and Leo Zhou applied the QAOA to the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. We showed how to analyze performance in the infinite size limit at any depth. Our work and others indicated that as depth increases with optimal parameters, the QAOA would approach the celebrated Parisi value. Recently the Open AI math dump, the conjecture that the QAOA would hit Parisi, was proven by the AI. I bet Jeffrey would have been surprised and impressed!”
Jeffrey Goldstone was a fellow of the American Physical Society Fellow, the Royal Society, and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and he was an honorary fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge.
His honors included the Guthrie Medal of the Institute of Physics, the Dannie Heineman Prize for Mathematical Physics of the APS, and with Stanley Mandelstam the Dirac Medal (1991) of the Abdus Salam International Centre for Theoretical Physics, awarded for “his fundamental clarification of the phenomenon of spontaneous symmetry violation in relativistic field theory.”
He is survived by his son Andrew Goldstone, associate professor of English at Rutgers University’s New Brunswick campus; his daughter-in-law Anne Dewitt, a clinical associate professor at New York University’s Gallatin School of Individualized Study; and his granddaughter, Helen. His family is planning a memorial in 2027.

candidato.titulo: Nvidia and Jensen Huang face class-action lawsuit after affair with alleged Chinese spy wipes $190 billion off company
candidato.resumo: Huang admitted to the extramarital affair over the weekend following reports that he was targeted by a suspected Chinese intelligence operative, Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen. US intelligence services claim she was acting as a honeypot, tasked with gathering information about American AI chips and influencing the... Read Entire Article

texto_fonte:
Sounding off: In what's turning out to be the most costly mistake ever, Nvidia and its CEO are now facing a class-action lawsuit from shareholders after Jensen Huang admitted he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Huang has confirmed that he was romantically involved with the woman, an admission that has already wiped around $190 billion off Nvidia's market cap.
Huang admitted to the extramarital affair over the weekend following reports that he was targeted by a suspected Chinese intelligence operative, Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen. US intelligence services claim she was acting as a honeypot, tasked with gathering information about American AI chips and influencing the Nvidia chief to push for China to get the company's most advanced processors.
In a letter to employees, Huang apologized to his wife, family, and colleagues, taking responsibility for his actions and promising to cooperate with an investigation.
Rosen Law Firm has now filed a class-action complaint against Nvidia and its CEO in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. It's been brought by individual investor Mark Kistenmacher and "on behalf of all persons similarly situated," covering those who purchased Nvidia stock between October 9 of last year and November 8 of this year.
The suit alleges that Nvidia and Huang deceived investors by making false and misleading statements regarding the CEO's relationship with Alice Huang.
A former executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed International, Alice Huang was reportedly monitored by US intelligence agencies after they concluded she had collaborated with Chinese intelligence. US authorities have also been investigating allegations that Megaspeed routed Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China through intermediaries.
 – Pix🔎 (@PixBuilds) November 9, 2026
Soon after The New York Times reported on Huang's contact with Alice Huang late last month, Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said in a statement that "the interactions Jensen had with Ms. Huang were not unusual or unexpected," adding that "meeting with customers is part of a CEO's job, and Jensen speaks with executives from thousands of customer companies every year."
The suit claims that Rizzo's statement was a deliberate falsehood intended to conceal the personal nature of the pair's relationship. It also cites Jensen Huang's comments in a Bloomberg interview, in which he said Nvidia's dealings with Megaspeed were "normal and not unusual."
The plaintiffs argue that the relationship raised national security questions about Nvidia's dealings with Megaspeed and that revealing it would have harmed the company's reputation and business prospects. They allege that concealing it led investors to buy shares at artificially inflated prices, only to suffer losses when Huang acknowledged the relationship and the stock dropped.
Other law firms are investigating the matter, so Nvidia could soon be spending some of the billions it's earning from the AI boom on legal fees.
Nvidia shares fell almost 5% following Huang's admission, wiping around $190 billion off its value in a single day. In the past month, its stock price has gone from $228 to $176, a drop of almost 23%.
Jensen's actions could have a bigger impact than lawsuits. With Nvidia's share price dropping and the company facing the prospect of losing its influential leader, some warn this could have set off a chain of events that ultimately pops the AI bubble. Unsurprisingly, the internet is having a field day.

candidato.titulo: Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy puts Nvidia’s China ambitions under scrutiny
candidato.resumo: Jensen Huang’s alleged affair with a suspected Chinese spy threatens to complicate Nvidia’s lobbying efforts to loosen U.S. chip export restrictions and maintain access to China’s lucrative AI market.

texto_fonte:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has never been quiet about his belief that the U.S. should continue selling AI chips to China, rather than shutting the country off from the technology. The revelation that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy threatens to complicate that argument.
The Financial Times reported Friday on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. Jensen Huang admitted to the affair and apologized in a memo to the company on Sunday. U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was recruited by Chinese intelligence to gather information about the CEO and influence the company’s efforts to loosen chip export restrictions.
Nvidia’s independent directors, working with outside legal counsel, are investigating the matter, and Congress is already demanding answers.
The controversy comes at a sensitive moment for Nvidia. Historically, China has been a big market for the company. It has shrunk in recent years due to strict U.S. export controls and an aggressive push by Beijing for domestic alternatives. In the three months ended July 26, Nvidia recorded $7.9 billion in revenue from customers headquartered in China, roughly 8% of total revenue.
Huang has repeatedly lobbied the U.S. government to expand access to China, and some of his persuasion tactics have been successful. Huang met repeatedly with President Donald Trump and administration officials last year; afterward, the government reversed restrictions on Nvidia’s H20 chips and allowed exports of its more powerful H200 processors.
On numerous occasions, Huang has publicly lamented export controls, calling them a “failure” at a conference last year and saying in May that it was “not wise” for the U.S. and China to create two distinct AI ecosystems. He has also warned that shutting Nvidia out of China’s compute market would enable the country to develop its own AI chips to challenge Nvidia internationally.
China is already moving in that direction. Reuters reported last week that about 600,000 H200 chips are being held in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment to mainland China. Beijing is pushing AI companies to prioritize buying chips from Chinese companies instead.
The idea that Huang needed any encouragement in the form of an attractive woman to push for greater access to China seems like a stretch, particularly because his lobbying efforts predate their reported meeting at an Nvidia event in early 2024. At the end of the day, Huang is a salesman trying to dominate one of the world’s biggest AI markets.
Still, the allegations involving Alice Huang open new scrutiny of the company’s business relationships and could taint any assurances Nvidia offers that it can prevent sensitive technology from reaching unauthorized customers.
Once made, rumors of questionable allegiances can be hard to shake. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly warned officials close to Trump earlier this year about Huang’s relationship with an alleged spy. Even if Nvidia’s investigation finds that Huang didn’t share secrets with his paramour, the question is whether he’ll be able to convince Washington that Nvidia can still responsibly do business with China.
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

candidato.titulo: New research explains why silicon outperforms thin film in the race for solar panel supremacy
candidato.resumo: Even the most promising technologies can fail to take off if governments, producers and suppliers, along with consumer and business demand, are not able to support their growth, according to new research by Bayes Business School.

texto_fonte:
New research explains why silicon outperforms thin film in the race for solar panel supremacy
Even the most promising technologies can fail to take off if governments, producers and suppliers, along with consumer and business demand, are not able to support their growth, according to new research by Bayes Business School.
The paper published in Organization Science, co-authored by Dr. Mara Guerra, senior lecturer in strategy at Bayes, and Professor Rajshree Agarwal of the University of Maryland, compared respective development pathways for silicon and thin-film technologies that grew the U.S. solar photovoltaics (PV) industry between the 1950s and the present day.
For many years, both technologies had their own strengths. Thin film had lower per-unit cost and versatility while silicon also benefited from falling costs and innovation, and there was no obvious front-runner. However, when demand finally took off in the late 2000s, silicon was in a better position to meet utilities' requirements at scale, reliably and cost-effectively.
The virtuous cycle of events that pressed home silicon's advantage is identified by the researchers as a "reinforcement loop." Established supply chains and manufacturing equipment helped silicon achieve scale, which then enhanced reliability, reputation and cost efficiency. This in turn attracted further interest, investment and demand.
By contrast, thin film had more customized supply chains and weaker economies of scale, making it less reliable and financially unsustainable and leading to a queue of market exits from investors and producers. Thin-film technology, according to the study, had been slowed down by "balancing loops."
At the end of the study period in 2020, silicon accounted for 91% of solar PV industry sales. While a similar number of solar cell producers entered into each technology during the period studied, three-quarters of thin-film companies exited—paving the way for silicon to dominate.
The research comprehensively explored a large range of industry news coverage, reports, market entrants' strategies, government interventions and investment history to uncover patterns and interdependencies with the fortunes of the two competing solar panel technologies.
Guerra said, "Our research strongly suggests that technologies do not just appear through innovation, but rely on interaction between a much wider group of actors, from manufacturers and equipment suppliers to governments, utilities and financiers.
"Silicon did not simply win the battle because it was the better technology. It won because it was better equipped to take advantage of an ecosystem that had developed around solar power as demand began to take off.
"Silicon solar PV's success has important wider implications for other emerging technologies. Developing a viable technology is only a small part of the challenge. Businesses and policymakers also need to understand whether the wider ecosystem—investors, activists, policymakers, consumers—is ready to support it at scale."
Publication details
Mara Guerra et al., Technology (Non)Emergence: How System Interdependencies Among Activities by Heterogeneous Actors Shaped Alternative Solar Technology Trajectories, Organization Science (2026). DOI: 10.1287/orsc.2022.17185

candidato.titulo: CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

texto_fonte:
CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents
WASHINGTON – Today, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) unveiled the updated cyber incident reporting form, an enhanced web-enabled questionnaire available on CISA’s Incident Reporting Portal for reporting cyber incidents. By improving data quality, the more robust form strengthens the effectiveness and efficiency of national cyber defense. For instance, the new form will help CISA correlate related cyber threat activity to identify a larger trend from what otherwise would appear as independent incidents.
The new cyber incident reporting form is guided by community feedback CISA has received over the years and the agency’s efforts to improve data quality that enables rapid yet thorough threat analysis. For example, questions about the type of incident are more comprehensive and seek more granular information, including whether the incident involved malware, social engineering, hacking techniques or an insider threat. Also, questions about observed activity now incorporate the MITRE ATT&CK® Framework, language about adversary behavior that is familiar to the cyber community.
“In the team sport of cybersecurity, one organization’s detection is another’s protection,” said Acting Executive Assistant Director for Cybersecurity Chris Butera. “As the national coordinator for critical infrastructure cybersecurity and resilience, CISA is able to leverage such incident reporting to identify emerging cyber campaigns, warn potential targets, and strengthen the Nation’s collective defense.”
While only federal civilian agencies are required to report, CISA encourages any organization that experiences a cyber incident to voluntarily report.
For more information, please visit the Frequently Asked Questions webpage.
###
About CISA
As the nation’s cyber defense agency and national coordinator for critical infrastructure security, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency leads the national effort to manage, uncover, and reduce risk to our digital and physical infrastructure Americans rely on every hour of every day.
Visit CISA.gov for more information and follow us on X, Facebook, LinkedIn, Instagram.
